title: Communicable and Non-Communicable Disease Control
description: Principles of disease control, surveillance and outbreak response, control of priority communicable diseases, immunisation, and prevention of non-communicable diseases.

topics.title: Principles of Disease Control
topics.summary: Control, elimination and eradication, the chain of infection, and levels of prevention.

notes.b: Control reduces disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity or mortality to a locally acceptable level with continued intervention. Elimination reduces incidence to zero in a defined geographical area (e.g. elimination of neonatal tetanus as a public health problem, measles elimination targets). Eradication is the permanent reduction of worldwide incidence to zero so interventions are no longer needed — achieved only for smallpox (1980) and rinderpest; polio and dracunculiasis (Guinea worm — Nigeria certified free in 2013) are close. Wild poliovirus was declared eradicated from Nigeria and Africa in 2020, though circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 persists. Eradicable diseases usually have no animal reservoir, an effective intervention and easy diagnosis.

The chain of infection links the agent, reservoir (human, animal, environment), portal of exit, mode of transmission (direct contact, droplet, airborne, vehicle-borne, vector-borne), portal of entry and susceptible host; breaking any link controls disease. Control measures target the reservoir (case finding, treatment, isolation, quarantine of contacts, animal control), transmission (sanitation, safe water, vector control, hand hygiene, PPE), and the host (immunisation, chemoprophylaxis, nutrition, health education). Levels of prevention: primordial (preventing risk factors emerging), primary (preventing disease onset — vaccination), secondary (early detection and treatment — screening), tertiary (limiting disability — rehabilitation) and quaternary (avoiding overmedicalisation). Herd immunity protects unvaccinated people when enough of the population is immune.

topics.title: Surveillance and Outbreak Investigation
topics.summary: Types of surveillance, IDSR, notifiable diseases and steps in outbreak investigation.

notes.b: Public health surveillance is the ongoing systematic collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination of health data for action. Types: passive (routine reports from facilities — cheap but under-reports), active (health workers seek cases — e.g. AFP surveillance for polio), sentinel (selected sites report detailed data — e.g. HIV sentinel surveys in antenatal clinics), syndromic (based on symptom patterns) and event-based surveillance (media, rumours, community reports). Nigeria uses Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) with immediately notifiable diseases (e.g. cholera, Lassa fever, measles, meningitis, yellow fever, AFP/polio, avian influenza, mpox, diphtheria) and weekly/monthly reportable diseases. Surveillance data are reported through SORMAS and DHIS2, and NCDC publishes situation reports.
k: Immediately notifiable: Lassa, cholera, measles, AFP

notes.b: An outbreak (epidemic) is the occurrence of cases in excess of normal expectancy. Steps: (1) prepare for fieldwork; (2) establish the existence of an outbreak (compare with baseline); (3) verify the diagnosis (clinical and laboratory); (4) construct a case definition (suspected, probable, confirmed — by person, place and time) and find cases systematically; (5) perform descriptive epidemiology (epidemic curve, spot maps, attack rates by person characteristics); (6) develop hypotheses; (7) evaluate hypotheses analytically (case–control or cohort study); (8) refine hypotheses and additional studies; (9) implement control and prevention measures (as early as possible — control measures should not wait for all steps); (10) communicate findings. The epidemic curve's shape indicates the type of outbreak: point-source (single sharp peak), continuous common-source, or propagated (person-to-person, successive peaks). An Emergency Operations Centre coordinates the response.
k: Point-source: single peak; propagated: successive peaks

topics.title: Control of Priority Communicable Diseases
topics.summary: Malaria, tuberculosis, HIV, cholera, Lassa fever and neglected tropical diseases.

notes.b: Nigeria bears the highest malaria burden in the world (about a quarter of global cases and deaths). Control: insecticide-treated nets (long-lasting ITNs), indoor residual spraying, seasonal malaria chemoprevention for children in the Sahel (SP + amodiaquine, July–October), intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp-SP), prompt testing with RDTs and treatment with ACTs, and the new malaria vaccines (RTS,S and R21, introduced in Nigeria in 2024). Tuberculosis: Nigeria is among the top TB burden countries with many missed cases; the DOTS strategy and End TB Strategy use active case finding, GeneXpert testing, treatment (2HRZE/4HR), TB preventive therapy and HIV integration. HIV: 95-95-95 targets (diagnosed, on ART, virally suppressed), test-and-treat, PMTCT, PrEP and condom promotion.

Cholera (Vibrio cholerae; outbreaks in rainy seasons and in IDP camps) is controlled by safe water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), case management with ORS and IV fluids, oral cholera vaccine and surveillance. Lassa fever (arenavirus; reservoir the multimammate rat Mastomys natalensis; peaks December–April; endemic in Edo, Ondo, Bauchi, Ebonyi) is controlled by rodent control, food storage, early diagnosis and ribavirin, and infection prevention and control in hospitals. Cerebrospinal meningitis (meningitis belt; MenAfriVac against serogroup A; recent serogroup C outbreaks; pentavalent Men5CV introduced). Neglected tropical diseases (onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma) are controlled by mass drug administration (ivermectin, albendazole, praziquantel, azithromycin) and WASH.

topics.title: Immunisation Programmes
topics.summary: Nigeria's routine schedule, cold chain, AEFI and strategies to improve coverage.

notes.b: Nigeria's routine immunisation schedule (National Programme on Immunisation): at birth — BCG, OPV0 and hepatitis B birth dose; 6, 10 and 14 weeks — pentavalent (DTP–HepB–Hib), PCV, OPV, rotavirus (6 and 10 weeks); 14 weeks — IPV; 6 months — vitamin A; 9 months — measles and yellow fever, plus meningococcal conjugate (in the meningitis belt) and IPV second dose; 15 months — measles second dose. HPV vaccine was introduced in 2023 for girls aged 9–14 years (single dose). Tetanus–diphtheria (Td) is given to women of childbearing age and in pregnancy. Supplementary immunisation activities (campaigns) complement routine immunisation. Coverage remains low in many northern states, with many 'zero-dose' children.

The cold chain keeps vaccines at +2 °C to +8 °C from manufacturer to recipient (OPV may be stored frozen at central levels). Heat-sensitive vaccines include OPV and measles; freeze-sensitive vaccines (pentavalent, HepB, PCV, IPV, Td) are damaged by freezing — the shake test detects freeze damage. Vaccine vial monitors (VVMs) change colour with cumulative heat exposure; discard vials when the inner square matches or is darker than the outer circle. Multi-dose vial policy: opened vials of some vaccines may be used for up to 28 days under proper conditions; reconstituted vaccines (BCG, measles, yellow fever) must be discarded after 6 hours or at the end of the session. Adverse events following immunisation (AEFI) must be reported and investigated. Strategies to improve coverage: reaching every ward, community engagement with traditional and religious leaders, reminder systems, tracking defaulters and integrating services.

topics.title: Prevention of Non-Communicable Diseases
topics.summary: NCD burden, shared risk factors, WHO best buys and screening programmes.

notes.b: Non-communicable diseases (cardiovascular disease, cancers, chronic respiratory disease, diabetes, and increasingly mental disorders) cause about 29% of deaths in Nigeria and rising — the double burden of disease alongside infections. Shared modifiable behavioural risk factors: tobacco use, harmful alcohol use, unhealthy diet (high salt, sugar, trans fats; low fruit and vegetables), and physical inactivity; metabolic risk factors: raised blood pressure (hypertension affects about 30% of Nigerian adults, often undiagnosed), overweight/obesity, raised blood glucose and raised lipids; plus air pollution. Urbanisation and changing lifestyles drive rising NCDs. The WHO STEPwise approach (STEPS) surveys risk factors.

WHO 'best buys' are cost-effective NCD interventions: tobacco taxation, smoke-free public places, graphic health warnings and advertising bans (Nigeria's National Tobacco Control Act 2015); alcohol taxes and availability restrictions; salt reduction; eliminating trans fats; sugar-sweetened beverage taxes (Nigeria introduced a ₦10/litre levy in 2022); public awareness on physical activity; drug therapy and counselling for people at high cardiovascular risk; and HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screening (VIA, HPV testing). The WHO HEARTS package and PEN (Package of Essential NCD interventions) strengthen primary care management of hypertension and diabetes, including task-sharing with nurses and CHEWs. Screening programmes: blood pressure, blood glucose, breast awareness and clinical breast examination, cervical screening.
